item.title: The Joy of Longing
item.description:
Fantasies

The Joy of Longing

Yearning for somewhere else doesn’t mean you’re in the wrong place.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Longing for distant places or other lives is not necessarily a sign of dissatisfaction with our own lives.
  • The German term fernweh describes our longing for distant places. It's the opposite of homesickness.
  • Our imagined selves can be seen as reminders that we're capable of wonder and reinvention.

Sometimes I'm driving down a highway when I pass a single farmhouse standing by itself, miles from another building, its porch light already glowing though the sun hasn't quite finished its work. For a few seconds, I live there. I imagine making soup in its kitchen. I know the names of the hawks. I have forgotten what day of the week it is.

The feeling passes as quickly as it arrived, but it has happened all my life: A lighthouse. A cottage in Ireland. An apartment over a bookshop. A train station with one lonely bench. I have briefly inhabited all of them.

For years I interpreted this as evidence that something was wrong. Maybe I had made poor choices. Maybe somewhere along the way I'd taken a wrong turn.

Philipp De Vries
Source: Used with permission/Philipp De Vries

Then, while recording my podcast 50 Words for Snow, where my co-host Emily Garces and I explore words that have no direct English equivalent, our German guest, Philipp De Vries, introduced us to the word fernweh. Literally, it means "far-pain," or a longing for distant places. It is the opposite of homesickness.

What struck me wasn't simply that another language had a word for a feeling I'd experienced. It was the possibility that I'd been interpreting that feeling all wrong.

We often treat longing like a diagnosis. If we keep imagining another life, perhaps our current one isn't enough. If we fantasize about living in a cabin in the woods or on a tiny Scottish island, maybe we're secretly trying to escape.

But what if longing isn't always pointing away from our lives? What if it is simply pointing toward our imagination?

I've started noticing that these little daydreams rarely leave me wanting to pack a suitcase. Instead, I return to my own life feeling slightly larger. The fantasy has stretched something inside me.

During our conversation, Philipp described fernweh as "more than escaping and less than manifesting." I loved that distinction. It isn't a plan. It isn't regret. It isn't dissatisfaction. It's a gentle reaching toward possibility.

The Lives We Never Live

The imagined woman in the lighthouse isn't asking me to abandon my life. The person living above the bookshop isn't criticizing my career. They are simply reminding me that I contain more versions of myself than the one currently answering emails, paying bills, and trying to remember where I left my keys.

For years I thought they represented roads not taken. Now I wonder if they're simply evidence that the imagination is doing exactly what it evolved to do: exploring possibilities without demanding that we choose them.

I've come to think of those distant places less as destinations than invitations. They invite me to remember that I am capable of curiosity, reinvention, and wonder. They remind me that another self is always possible, not because I need a different address, but because there is always another way of seeing.

Maybe that's the real gift of fernweh. The longing for another place doesn't necessarily mean we've chosen the wrong one. It may simply mean that we haven't stopped imagining.

As long as there is one more road disappearing into the hills, one more porch light glowing in the distance, one more train slowing into a town I'll probably never visit, I can remember something that took me a long time to learn: My life is larger than the one I happen to be living.

item.title: New Study: 21 Million Americans Now Use Cannabis Daily, Despite the Risks
item.description:
Alcoholism

New Study: 21 Million Americans Now Use Cannabis Daily, Despite the Risks

New SAMHSA data show how prevalent cannabis addiction has become as well.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • More than 21 million Americans now use cannabis daily or nearly daily
  • Frequent cannabis use can produce tolerance, withdrawal, and an addiction-shaped brain state.
  • Learning to smoke or vape may make switching between cannabis (THC) and tobacco (nicotine) easier.
  • Cannabis odor can become a conditioned cue, triggering craving before conscious awareness.

A few weeks ago, I described what happens inside the brain when cannabis is used every day. Daily use does not simply produce a series of separate episodes of intoxication. Over time, it can shift the brain toward an adapted “on THC” operating state—one persisting between doses and that users may experience as “feeling normal” rather than feeling high.

Cigarette smokers know a similar dynamic. Nicotine may seem calming, but often it is actually relieving the withdrawal and irritability produced by the previous cigarette.

Newly released federal data now show just how large the population living with near-continuous cannabis exposure has become.

What the 2025 National Survey on Drug Use and Health Found

The 2025 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, focused on Americans aged 12 and older, reports that cannabis is now the most-commonly-used substance daily or nearly daily in the United States.

An estimated 21.4 million people used cannabis on at least 300 days in 2025. By comparison, 19.9 million smoked cigarettes daily, 17.5 million vaped nicotine daily, and 17.2 million drank alcohol daily or nearly daily. This is an important addiction milestone.

The survey also estimates that 19.3 million Americans had a past-year cannabis use disorder—the most prevalent drug use disorder other than alcohol use disorder.

But this new data does not mean that cannabis has surpassed alcohol in terms of total use or harm. Alcohol’s user base remains roughly three times larger, and its mortality and organ-damage burden are far greater. This does, however, mean that cannabis users are much more likely than alcohol users to use the substance frequently: Nearly half of past-month cannabis users used the drug at least 300 days a year, compared with about 13 percent of past-month alcohol users who drank on 20 or more days a month.

The cannabis frequent-use population has grown by 3.7 million since 2022. Cannabis-policy researcher Jonathan Caulkins found that between 2008 and 2022, past-year use increased 120 percent, while cannabis-use days increased 218 percent. It's not simply that more people are trying cannabis. Existing users are using it more often—exactly what we might expect as an addictive drug becomes more available, potent, normalized, and commercially promoted.

Why I Keep Coming Back to Cigarettes

Cannabis and cigarettes are not equally addictive or equally lethal; nicotine remains a faster and more reliable producer of dependence. But we should remember the old duck test: If it looks like a duck, walks like a duck, and quacks like a duck, it probably is a duck.

The behavioral architecture of daily cannabis use resembles cigarette smoking. It involves tolerance, withdrawal, cue-driven behavior, use to relieve withdrawal, and difficulty quitting. Not every daily user meets the criteria for a use disorder. However, a recent Australian study found that more than a third of people prescribed medical cannabis met the current criteria for cannabis use disorder, not surprisingly driven primarily by those not using cannabis as prescribed.

If a drug is used daily, produces tolerance and withdrawal, and becomes difficult to stop, the relationship has taken an addiction-shaped form—whether the person calls it medicine, a wind-down ritual, or simply part of the day.

Regular cannabis or THC use produces receptor downregulation, withdrawal, and a new on-cannabis brain—a baseline that daily users may come to mistake for normal.

This is where the brain and survey data meet. Cannabis may appear to help someone sleep, relax, eat, or “feel normal” when it is partly relieving withdrawal from the previous dose. Among the 21.4 million people using cannabis at least 300 days a year, many have given that adapted brain state ample time to become established.

Cannabis vs Cigarettes vs Alcohol
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

When Smoke Becomes a Cue—and a Bridge

Cannabis smoke and odor have become part of the public environment. For someone with cannabis use disorder—or someone trying to stop using—a cannabis smell coming from a sidewalk, concert, or apartment hallway may not be neutral. Once paired repeatedly with intoxication or relief, odor can become a conditioned cue, evoking craving before the person consciously identifies the trigger. Pervasive tobacco smoke once played much the same role.

Seeing someone smoke can also trigger cravings. The act of smoking is learned with suppression of cough reflex, inhalation, airway sensations, rapid drug delivery, and the expectation of an immediate brain effect.

An outdoor cannabis odor may be a craving or relapse cue even when it delivers no meaningful THC dose. Dense secondhand smoke in a poorly ventilated space is different: It may provoke a pharmacologic exposure and also contains fine particles and toxic products of combustion.

More than 20 years ago, my colleagues and I described the close relationship between marijuana and tobacco use. At that time, tobacco usually came first. Today, cannabis may come first, making later tobacco use feel easier and more familiar. Vaping further blurs the boundary: The same device and inhalation ritual can deliver nicotine, THC, or both.

Progression is not inevitable, and individual vulnerability matters. But the critical step may be learning to inhale a drug for rapid brain delivery—almost an injection without a needle. The modern concern is not simply one gateway drug leading to another, but a shared behavior that makes movement between nicotine and THC increasingly easy.

What the Headlines Do, and Do Not, Mean

Daily or near-daily cannabis use means at least 300 days of use during the past year, whereas other drugs refer to the past month. The small differences between cannabis and cigarettes may not be statistically significant—the survey measured days, not THC dose or potency. Most importantly, frequency is not diagnosis. Frequent users and people with cannabis use disorder overlap, but are not identical groups.

The new survey does not prove that every daily user is addicted. It shows that the population at risk of living in an addiction-shaped, adapted brain state is disturbingly large—and growing.

But the old “duck test” applies: When cannabis use produces tolerance, withdrawal, craving, repetitive use, and difficulty quitting—features long associated with nicotine addiction—we should be willing to call the pattern addiction-like.

Commercialization Is Part of the Explanation

A 2026 international review found that commercialized cannabis markets were associated with increased use and potency, more cannabis use disorder, and more psychosis-related hospital care.

That may ring familiar from our experiences with tobacco, alcohol, and gambling. An industry’s largest profits rarely come from occasional users. They derive from those using a product frequently or daily. Once a business model depends on heavy users, it is sales-driven and can be in an adverse position to public health.

Cannabis has become a commercial industry offering flowers, edibles, vapes, beverages, and high-potency concentrates. Advertising, discounts, loyalty programs, and promotional pricing may encourage frequent use.

Where the Leaf Leads

Cannabis is not more lethal than alcohol or cigarettes. It does not produce cigarette smoking’s cancer burden or alcohol’s overdose, injury, and organ-damage profile. But “less lethal than alcohol or tobacco” is not the same as “medicine" and not the same as “safe” when increasingly potent and addicting THC-containing products are being used frequently, at will, and by a population of at least 21.4 million individuals.

This is not a story about cannabis passing alcohol or cigarettes. It’s a story about many Americans moving in a short time from occasional use to an everyday, tolerance-and-withdrawal-shaped relationship with a drug. The same broad pattern defined cigarette smoking at its peak.

item.title: Big Tech Believes in You
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Big Tech Believes in You

Personal Perspective: Big Tech believes in you the way a con artist believes in his mark.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Meta's new AI ad says it believes in people. We should consider what that really means.
  • Big Tech's playbook: Manufacture the problem, then sell the solution.
  • "Supernormal stimuli" explains what tech ads never will.
Source: Image created by ChatGPT

Meta released a commercial this summer telling us it believes in people. "Some people will have you believe AI will make us less connected," the narrator says. "We couldn't disagree more." Twenty-two years and 3.5 billion users after Facebook launched, the ad tells us, the company's technology has changed, but its intentions never have. "Call us optimists. Call us dreamers. Call us whatever the hell you want. We're betting on people, and we like those odds."

I agree that Meta is betting on people, but not in the way this commercial implies. And it's not just Meta. Anthropic ran a campaign this summer built around the question "can AI be trusted," arcing toward hope by the end. OpenAI has its own version of this pitch. The entire industry has converged on the same message at the same moment: Don't worry, we believe in you. I think these companies genuinely do believe in people, the way a con artist believes in his mark.

The ads want you to hear "we believe in people" as a statement about your resilience and your capacity for connection. What it actually means, if you look at what these companies have built over two decades, is closer to this: We believe you are predictable. We believe you are exploitable. We believe that when we build something compelling enough, you will choose it over the healthier, harder thing, almost every time. And we like those odds, because we've tested them for years and they've made us some of the most profitable companies ever to exist on Earth.

Meta recently lost a social media addiction trial in California and a child safety case in Mexico, both built on the argument that its platforms were designed to hook young users before they had the cognitive equipment to resist them. You don't get sued for that by accident. You get sued for it because engagement systems worked exactly as intended, and they worked best on brains that hadn't finished developing the machinery to see it coming.

The part of you these companies are selling to

As a clinical psychologist, I've spent nearly 30 years listening to people describe similar experiences in a hundred forms. They know the thing isn't good for them. They do it anyway. They watch porn for hours past the point of pleasure. They check the app again after swearing they were done. None of this is a character flaw. It's what happens when a nervous system built for scarcity and small tribes meets a stimulus engineered by people with unlimited data on exactly what your brain finds irresistible. Evolutionary psychologists call this a supernormal stimulus, something that hijacks an instinct so effectively that we can prefer the engineered thing to the real one. We are running very old software in a very new environment, and the companies building that environment know it better than we know ourselves.

That's what the commercials leave out. Meta's shows rooftop dancing, kids in a lake, friends embracing after time apart, and never mentions that its fortune was built on the version of you that can't stop scrolling at midnight, that compares its life to strangers' highlight reels until something in your chest goes hollow. These companies didn't create our vulnerabilities. Evolution did. But they found them, mapped them, and built a business on them, and now they want credit for allegedly believing in the very people they've spent two decades studying like a lab.

The fire and the extinguisher

Here's what infuriates me. Two decades of social platforms have coincided with rising loneliness and isolation, especially among the generation that grew up inside them. Now the same industry says AI will finally deliver the connection its earlier products promised and didn't. This isn't a new chapter; it's the oldest trick available. Sell the fire, then sell the extinguisher.

What worries me, perhaps even more than the manipulation, is the tool being offered as the fix. The thing making us lonelier is now the proposed solution—more advanced tech. The capability you'd need to see through an ad like this, to sit with discomfort, question a compelling narrative, and notice your own patterns and interrupt them, is precisely what gets weaker the more we hand our thinking to something else. These companies aren't just betting we'll stay distracted. They're betting the next tools make it even harder to notice that we are.

The answer is not more willpower. Telling an exhausted person to simply try harder against a system built by people with more data on their habits than they have on themselves isn't helpful; it's just another burden on someone already running on empty. But there's something that isn't willpower and still works, and it's what I watch happen in a therapy room: Understanding the mechanism changes your relationship to it, even before your behavior catches up. A person who believes their midnight scrolling is a personal failing spends most of their energy managing shame. A person who understands the product was engineered, deliberately, to exploit exactly what they're feeling right now, spends that energy differently. Naming the trap accurately isn't a failure. For a depleted person, it's often the first move available.

I don't believe AI will make us more connected because an ad says so over footage of rainbows and reunions. I believe these companies know precisely what they're betting on, because they built the algorithms themselves. The future isn't a mystery. It's a pattern we've already lived through.

I've been writing this blog for years because I care about the future of intimacy. Technology is already reshaping it. What I hope is for people to keep choosing each other anyway, not because the human version is nobler, but because it's the one we're actually built for. A supernormal stimulus can hijack the craving, but it’s unlikely to satisfy it. That gap is where the loneliness lives, and no amount of AI is going to close it, because it isn't designed to. It's designed to keep you coming back.

item.title: Betting on the Future
item.description:
Decision-Making

Betting on the Future

How contingency contracts turn disagreement into opportunity.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Contingency contracts turn disagreement about the future into structured opportunity.
  • They work by distributing risk, testing predictions, and aligning incentives.
  • They turn "no" into "not yet."

It began decades ago when a woman in her first year of law school wandered into a guest lecture about a newly emerging field called employment law. It wasn’t labor law, and it wasn’t wage‑and‑hour law; it was something new, something still forming, something focused on the relationship between employers and employees. The idea lodged itself in her mind. She enrolled in the first employment law class her school ever offered, went home, and told her husband—then a young associate finally earning a decent salary—that he and his firm ought to develop a plaintiff‑side employment law practice. He admired her conviction, but he had no authority to make such a thing happen, and the litigation partner he reported to was a named partner, respected, formidable, and not easily persuaded to try something untested.

He filed the idea away.

Months later, a law school friend approached him with an unexpected request: Would he represent the friend’s wife in a pregnancy discrimination case? Suddenly, the abstract idea had become a concrete possibility. He took the matter to the partner, made his best pitch, and waited. The partner listened, paused, and shook his head. Employment law was too new, damages too uncertain, and the risk too high.

This is the moment where most people lose the first negotiation with themselves. They hear "no," and they retreat. But he had already learned something essential—something he would later write about in his Power & Influence column—that "no" is simply the first two letters of "not yet." Most people negotiate against themselves long before they ever reach another person, talking themselves out of asking again. He didn’t. He paused, regrouped, and reframed.

What he said next stopped the conversation cold: "Take the case and stop paying me a salary. If I win, I'll take a pre‑negotiated percentage of the fee."

It was not bravado. Inside, he was anything but calm. His wife, still in her first year of law school, was prohibited from working. His income was their only income. He had never practiced employment law. And if the case failed—if the jury didn't believe the story, if the law didn't hold, if the company prevailed—he would earn exactly zero dollars. The partner stared at him, asked whether he was sure, and waited, giving him one last chance to retreat. He didn't. He confirmed the offer, steadying himself as he did, and only then did the partner take it to the other partners for deliberation and ultimately agree.

It was a contingency agreement in its purest form: a structure designed for moments when people disagree about risk, value, or the future itself. The case went forward. The associate worked without pay, poured himself into the litigation, and ultimately won at trial, purportedly the earliest successful pregnancy discrimination verdict in California, and one of the first in the country. The judgment was collected, the contingency fee was paid, and the risk he had taken transformed into opportunity. The win created a financial windfall for both the firm and the young couple, launched them as employment law experts, and set in motion a trajectory that would eventually lead to nationally recognized success and, years later, the invitation to launch their own firm under remarkably favorable circumstances.

And by the way, that woman and that young associate? They're Linda and Craig—the two halves of what our students affectionately call "The Barki," yours truly, the authors of this blog.

Why Contingency Contracts Matter

That case didn't just change our careers; it revealed something fundamental about how people handle uncertainty. When parties disagree about the future, they often argue about whose prediction is right. Contingency contracts offer a different path, one that turns disagreement into structure and structure into opportunity.

To make the concept clearer, consider a simple triad we often use in our classrooms and executive sessions because it captures the essence of why these agreements work:

  • They distribute risk.
  • They test predictions.
  • They align performance with incentives.

When parties disagree about what will happen next, a contingency contract gives each side a way to act on its convictions without forcing premature compromise.

When the Bet Pays Off

After the 1984 Northridge earthquake, two major I‑10 freeway bridges collapsed, costing the Los Angeles economy an estimated $1 million per day in lost productivity. Construction projects are notorious for delays, so negotiators crafted one of the most famous contingency incentives in U.S. infrastructure history: a $200,000‑per‑day bonus for early completion. The contractor finished the project in 66 days, 74 days ahead of schedule. That is the power of a contingency contract; it turns urgency into motivation and prediction into performance.

But contingency agreements aren’t limited to multimillion‑dollar infrastructure projects or high‑stakes litigation. They appear in everyday life, often unnoticed. Consider a workplace performance bonus: A manager and employee disagree about how ambitious a quarterly sales target should be. The employee believes the market is soft; the manager believes it’s ripe. A contingency agreement bridges the gap. If the employee hits the higher target, the bonus is paid; if the market underperforms, the employee’s baseline salary remains protected. It is a small, familiar example of the same principle: Disagreement becomes structure, and structure becomes opportunity.

The Psychology Behind the Bet

Contingency contracts work because they correct for predictable human biases. Optimism bias leads people to overestimate positive outcomes. Overconfidence leads them to believe their predictions are more accurate than they are. Risk asymmetry means each side fears different losses. Prediction error is simply part of being human. A contingency contract doesn’t eliminate these biases; it harnesses them. It rewards disciplined optimism and penalizes wishful thinking. It forces both sides to confront the future honestly.

The Negotiator’s Takeaway

Contingency contracts are not just legal tools; they are negotiation superpowers. They reward accuracy, encourage honesty, and transform uncertainty into opportunity. They remind us that sometimes the best way to resolve disagreement is not to eliminate risk, but to share it wisely.

The Barki Challenge

Identify one disagreement in your life right now, professional or personal. Ask yourself whether a contingency agreement could turn that disagreement into a shared bet on the future. If the answer is yes, sketch the terms. You may discover that the disagreement wasn’t a barrier at all; it was an opportunity waiting to be structured.

Conclusion

The story we began with wasn’t just about a case. It was about a bet, one that carried real financial risk, real uncertainty, and real consequences for two young people who had more conviction than leverage. That bet changed the trajectory of our careers and, in time, shaped the lives of thousands of students, clients, and readers. Contingency contracts are, at their core, wagers on the future. They reward courage, clarity, and disciplined optimism. They turn “no” into “not yet,” and “not yet” into the beginning of everything that follows.

item.title: Normal Aging Brains Undergo Alteration, Not Deterioration
item.description:
Aging

Normal Aging Brains Undergo Alteration, Not Deterioration

Healthy older brains may exceed some cognitive functions of young brains.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Crystallized intelligence usually increases in the normal brain as one ages.
  • Wisdom differs widely between individuals of different ages and is not a necessary consequence of older age.
  • On memory tests, elders tend to perform best in the early morning, with performance declining by afternoon.

While clinical research is awash in studies comparing normal brains with brains affected by various diseases, comparisons of normal brains at a younger age with normal brains three or four decades older are less frequently encountered.

For one thing, as a person advances in age, their brain is increasingly likely to demonstrate some pathological change. Among people in their 80s, for instance, somewhere north of 70 percent will show at autopsy some of the pathological features of degenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer’s. (This is not the same thing as saying that they have Alzheimer’s disease, because some proportion of these people with mild pathological brain changes may perform perfectly normally when tested in their later years.) But since the percentage of 80-year-olds with signs of brain pathology is that high, one has to avoid comparing a normal brain of a 20- to 40-year-old with a 60-year-old diseased brain. Extra caution is needed to ensure that the elderly brain is indeed normal for age.

In volunteer subjects in their 20s and 30s, the estimation of normality is easy: Acceptable performance in school, healthy socialization patterns, and, later, work achievement can serve as proxies for normal cognitive function. If you restrict the upper limit of the comparison group to 60 years of age, external markers of achievement are also easily discerned—success over a long career coupled with a stable emotional history and general life satisfaction can serve as acceptable indicators of healthy cognitive function. In both age categories, any remaining doubts about brain normality can be resolved by psychological testing and brain imaging.

Alteration, Not Deterioration

Overall, with normal aging, mental performance abilities undergo alterations, rather than deterioration. Take intelligence, for instance. Fluid intelligence—the ability to quickly manipulate information, detect novel patterns, and respond correctly to new and challenging information—tends to function best earlier in life, with a decline accompanying aging.

In contrast, crystallized intelligence—accumulated knowledge, vocabulary, familiarity with facts along with skills acquired in higher education and lengthy experience—usually increases in the normal brain as one progresses from young adulthood into middle age and beyond.

A 65-year-old man or woman may know more words and remain capable of making fine, often subtle, distinctions between words than someone 30 or 40 years younger. This is based on the older person’s greater opportunities over the years to acquire an organized knowledge in specialized areas such as law or medicine.

For example, when you consult a law firm or medical practice about a complicated legal or medical problem, you’re likely to end up talking to someone with vast experience, knowledge, and appreciation of legal principles or, alternately, an in-depth understanding of medicine. Such an understanding takes years to establish. The longer the lawyer and doctor have been practicing law or medicine, respectively, the more knowledge and experience they have accrued.

In terms of emotions, differences are also apparent. Adults, in general, respond to negative emotions less intensely and recall past events more positively. This is especially true among healthy, well-educated middle-class individuals. Generally, similar findings are not as dependably present among people with less education and fewer resources. Further, elders often spend less time ruminating over negative experiences and take the “long view.” This can lead to superior performance in emotional or interpersonal contexts: "It just doesn't mean that much to me to get all wrought up about something I can't do anything about" is the typical response from a mature elder. In fact, if asked, most elders rate their ability to control negative emotions and behaviors as superior to their younger counterparts.

One factor in particular may negatively influence an older person’s cognitive performance. Testing of cognition, especially memory, is experienced as stressful by older people in ways that rarely affect their younger counterparts. “Do I have Alzheimer’s disease?” is a natural worry of an older person when tested, but rarely even occurs to a younger testee.

Since older people have been around for a longer period of time, they have acquired expertise in widely scattered areas of everyday living. A normally aging brain can often outperform a younger one when it comes to such things as understanding interpersonal complexity, appreciating that solutions to problems are rarely satisfactory to everyone concerned, recognizing interpersonal patterns leading to conflict, and drawing upon lifetime experiences when faced with seemingly insoluble problems or difficult choices. While these qualities of the maturing brain are sometimes labeled the “wisdom of the aged,” we have to be cautious here. Wisdom differs widely between individuals of different ages and is not a necessary consequence of increased chronological age.

As a general principle of learning, the older brain will often be unable to recall fine details while retaining the capacity to perceive the gist (the main point or essence of something read or written. “The so-called gist of an autobiographical event is not only spared with normal aging, but also well adapted to serve memory-guided behavior in older age,” according to Matthew D. Grilli, a psychologist at the University of Arizona.

Time-of-Day Effects

It makes a great deal of difference at what time of day testing is carried out (the so-called time-of-day effect). Worldwide research reveals that older and younger adults are attuned to different circadian (about 24 hours) arousal cycles. In general, older people awaken early and achieve their peak cognitive performance in the morning, while younger adults are cognitively at their best later in the day. Although this sounds like a generality, since there are exceptions, there is research to back it up:

On tests of memory, elders tend to perform at their best in the early morning, with performance declining by the afternoon. Younger adults, in contrast, perform at their best from later in the morning onward. In addition to memory, the most affected areas involve attention, executive function, and motor control.

Bottom line: Failure to take time differences into account when carrying out testing procedures may result in both over- and underestimation of cognitive performance. In a study on the optimal time of day for testing in light of the circadian differences found between younger and older brains, the authors conclude, “The full abilities of older adults may not be known—and will not be until circadian arousal patterns at times of testing are in synchrony in both younger and older adults.”

item.title: What Homer Can Teach Us About Ghosting
item.description:
Ghosting

What Homer Can Teach Us About Ghosting

Why being ignored hurts so much.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Ghosting hurts because it withdraws something more fundamental than love: recognition.
  • Homer's Argos reminds us that our deepest longing is simply to be seen and remembered.
  • Two of the world's greatest epics arrive at the same profound truth about fidelity.
Argos is the first to recognise Odysseus upon his return to Ithaca—and then dies.
Source: Neel Burton. AI generated.

The reunion of Odysseus and Argos occupies barely 40 lines, yet it is one of the most moving episodes in Homer’s Odyssey.

After 20 years away, Odysseus returns to Ithaca disguised as a beggar. Outside the palace lies his old hunting dog, Argos, blind, flea-ridden, and abandoned on a dung heap. Recognising his master, the dog lifts his head, gives a final wag of his tail—and dies.

Christopher Nolan greatly expanded Argos’ role in his film adaptation, showing the dog ageing under the neglect and abuse of the suitors. Many cinemagoers, myself included, found the brief reunion between dog and master to be the film’s most moving scene. Nolan has said that Argos was one of the elements that drew him to the project, even describing the epic as the "ultimate dog movie."

The Greek Dog

Why does this scene move us so deeply? There are many reasons. But one of the deepest is that Argos fulfils one of our most fundamental human longings: the longing to be recognised. Long before we seek fame or deeds, we seek to be known. Friends delight in being understood without explanation. Lovers hope to be recognised beneath the depredations of time. One of the quietest forms of suffering is not to be hated, but to be overlooked—to become as if invisible.

That is why being ghosted can be so painful. It is not merely rejection, but the withdrawal of recognition: the feeling that someone who once knew you now behaves as though you no longer existed. Argos does the opposite.

After 20 years of disguises and transformations, Argos alone recognises the man who once gave his name as "Nobody." The old dog sees beyond age and suffering—and Athena’s best work—to the man he has always known. Odysseus weeps for the dog, but he weeps also for himself. For 20 years, he has been all things to all men. Then, for one fleeting moment, someone recognises the one man beneath all the disguises.

The Indian Dog

Homer was not alone in seeing something profound in a dog’s fidelity. The Mahabharata, along with the Ramayana, is one of India’s two great epics. At the end of the Mahabharata, after the great war has been fought and every earthly hope has been shattered, the five Pandava brothers journey to Mount Meru, followed only by a stray dog. One by one, they fall on the ascent, leaving only the eldest, King Yudhisthira, to arrive at the gates of heaven.

The god Indra invites Yudhisthira into heaven, but refuses to admit the dog. Yudhisthira turns away, explaining that he cannot bring himself to abandon his faithful companion. At this, the dog reveals himself as none other than Dharma (cosmic order, duty, right way of living), and Yudhisthira is reunited with his brothers in Heaven.

Like Argos, the dog embodies something much greater than himself. By remaining faithful to faithfulness, Yudhisthira proves himself worthy of Heaven and saves his clan.

One Lesson

The two stories mirror one another. In Homer, it is the dog who remains faithful to a man. In the Mahabharata, it is just as much the man. Yet both honour the same virtue. Homer and the authors of the Mahabharata independently arrived at the same intuition, namely, that the fidelity of a dog is not merely an animal instinct. It is a revelation.

The irony, certainly in Homer, is that Argos remembers better than we do—better even than Penelope. Anyone who has ever ghosted, or been ghosted, may find themselves asking: Are we better than dogs?

Neel Burton is author of The Meaning of Myth.

item.title: In Managing AI, It’s All About Media Psychology
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

In Managing AI, It’s All About Media Psychology

Media psychology shapes everything from decision-making to emotional well-being.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • The amplified insinuation of AI into our daily lives continues apace.
  • As AI continues to evolve, it is crucial to thoughtfully navigate its social integration.
  • Both marketers and criminals use reward and instant-feedback techniques to trigger dopamine release.
Theories in Media Psychology
Source: Luskin International, with permission

Artificial intelligence (AI) is intertwined with our daily lives, from personal assistants on Apple Watches, iPhones, and tablets to chatbots offering customer service to drones increasingly changing the nature of war. Because AI manifests in technology, engineers tend to think about how many technical features can be included or added: more power, touch screens, and even more buttons. At the consumer level, insufficient thought may be given to insightfully understanding and simplifying the intuitive media psychology influence on AI technology use.

As the new president of Philips Interactive Media, the first TV/computer remotes I inherited in developing TV-based CD had more than 10 buttons on every controller because the digital engineers wanted to maximize the "buttonograpy." I argued for only an intuitive thumb stick and two buttons to control all features. For a period of time, we built the two-button version, and so did much of the gaming industry, and the response was dramatic. Within a year after my departure from Philips, engineering-dominated thinking reverted to maximizing the multibutton versions, which is still much of what we find today. This highlights issues amplified by understanding the psychological response of the average person on their phone, TV, watch, iPad, and other consumer devices. My point is simply about highlighting the importance of ease of use and user convenience. Ask yourself how intuitive the controller on each of your devices is. This prompted me to highlight the phrase, “It’s about the media psychology, stupid!” (a play on James Carville’s iconic phrase, “It's the economy, stupid!").

It’s about the media psychology

As AI continues to evolve, it is crucial to thoughtfully navigate its social integration.

Examples highlighting the media psychology influence on behaviors, beliefs, and decisions include:

  1. Social Engineering and Cognitive Bias. Attackers use principles like authority bias, scarcity, and reciprocity to trick users into revealing passwords, clicking malicious links, or transferring money. For example, phishing emails may mimic trusted sources or create urgency to overcome skepticism.
  2. AI-Powered Personalized Content. AI analyzes browsing, search, and social media data to create tailored content that reinforces existing beliefs, nudging users toward specific products or ideologies. This is used by marketers or criminals to shape opinions.
  3. Gamification and Dopamine Loops. The same marketers or criminals use reward and instant feedback to trigger dopamine release, encouraging repeated engagement. Stimulating dopamine release is common in social media, gaming, and streaming apps, in efforts to establish addictive use
  4. Scarcity and Fear of Missing Out. Social media and e-commerce sites highlight limited-time offers and amplify trending items or exclusivity of content to create urgency and immediate response, leveraging the human need for social connection.
  5. Deepfakes and Misinformation. AI-generated deepfake videos or images are used to simulate real people saying or doing things they never did, thereby creating false narratives that exploit trust.
  6. Manipulating User Interfaces: This includes design choices such as misleading buttons or confusing navigation to create decision fatigue and make users perform actions they might not otherwise choose, such as subscribing to services or sharing personal data.

These are only a few examples of how media psychology can be a tool for good or bad in understanding human behavior.

Media psychology shapes everything from our decision-making to our emotional well-being

More teaching about media psychology is needed in technical courses, and more certificates, courses, and degree programs in media psychology are needed at colleges and universities. Education about the media psychology of AI has become critical because of its growing influence.

Society for Media Psychology and Technology
Source: APA Media Psychology Div., with permission

The American Psychological Association, Media Psychology Division 46, Society for Media Psychology and Technology works to sharpen the focus of media psychology issues, possibilities, and promise. The society offers a gathering center for those pursuing insights and collegiality in media psychology.

As the insinuation of AI into our daily lives continues apace, it is important to “pay attention” to understanding and awareness of the addictive and manipulative nature of social media. Beware of the media psychology of the job offer, the lottery, the beneficiary, online dating, repair scams, charity requests, and robocall sales scams, just to highlight a few areas of concern. It is up to each of us as individuals, and those in education, health care, commerce, business, government, and the military to ensure that we share and use our insights productively and ethically. Simply stated, as AI continues to grow, please be aware of the paraphrase of Carville’s admonition: “It's the media psychology, stupid!”

item.title: New Ways to Deal With the Inner Critic
item.description:
Self-Help

New Ways to Deal With the Inner Critic

Learn to quiet the negative voice that sabotages you.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Many of us have an Inner Critic, a persistent negative voice that tells us we're not good enough.
  • We can develop an Inner Critic when we didn't get the nurturing support we needed as children.
  • Research reveals how you can keep the Inner Critic from sabotaging you.
Source: Peter Ziegler/Pixabay

You may have a persistent negative voice in your mind, especially when you’re doing something new, make a mistake, or feel anxious and uncertain. This Inner Critic says, “You never do anything right,” “You’re always messing up,” “You’re not good enough.”

In her new book, The Power of Authenticity, psychologist Michelle Chappel likens the Inner Critic’s voice to a talk radio station that drones on with negative messages, undermining our confidence and our ability to flourish (Chappel, 2026).

We can develop an Inner Critic if our parents or caregivers didn’t give us the nurturing support we needed. Research has traced many cases to childhood abuse or neglect (Mao et al., 2026; Sajjadi et al., 2023). The Inner Critic often echoes critical words we heard as children (Sokova et al., 2025), and we begin to feel that something is wrong with us.

But you don’t have to live with the Inner Critic. Research reveals how you can keep it from sabotaging you.

How to Overcome the Inner Critic

1. Mindfully notice it. As Chappel (2026) explains, the Inner Critic activates the amygdala, our brain’s alarm center. Plunging us into fight, flight, or freeze, it can keep us from thinking clearly and moving forward in life. Becoming mindful of the Inner Critic reduces its power over us (Sokova et al., 2025).

To detach from it further, you might even give it a comical name: “There’s that gremlin again.” The point here is to recognize that it’s not you, not true, but an old, conditioned reaction.

2. Put something positive in its place. Chappel (2026) recommends listening to uplifting music or doing something you love, like painting or running, which can put you into a flow state.

Another possibility is to use a positive affirmation or mantra (a spiritual word or phrase). Research has shown that when veterans with PTSD chose a mantram, practiced it, and then used it whenever they felt triggered, this practice significantly decreased their anxiety and negative feelings (Bormann et al., 2013). If a mantram practice can help people deal with the intrusive assaults of PTSD, it could also help you overcome the inner critic.

3. Practice self-compassion. New research shows how replacing the negative voice of the Inner Critic with the kind and supportive voice of self-compassion can help us with a range of challenges. One study shows how self-compassion can help us overcome negative emotional reactions and depressive symptoms from stress at work (Devenis-Meares, 2026).

Another study (Mao et al., 2026) shows that self-compassion can not only overcome the Inner Critic but even protect young people from intentionally hurting themselves. A qualitative study reveals that self-compassion can silence the Inner Critic and also lead to greater emotional resilience, self-acceptance, and empowerment (Sokova et al., 2025).

Psychologist Kristin Neff’s three steps to self-compassion are:

  1. Mindfully acknowledge what you’re feeling,
  2. Realize that it’s only human to feel this way, and
  3. Treat yourself kindly as you would a dear friend (Neff, 2011; Neff & Miyagawa, 2026).

Self-compassion can help you replace the critical voice with a kind, supportive inner voice.

So the next time you find yourself facing the Inner Critic, you can try:

  • Mindfully noticing the inner critic’s voice and detaching from it,
  • Replacing it with something positive,
  • Giving yourself self-compassion.

Mindfully changing your habitual thoughts from the Inner Critic with these three practices can make a positive difference in your life.

This post is for informational purposes and should not substitute for psychotherapy with a qualified professional.

item.title: Clinical Wisdom: Hidden Secrets of the Therapeutic Alliance
item.description:
Therapy

Clinical Wisdom: Hidden Secrets of the Therapeutic Alliance

How what happens (and doesn't happen) in the therapy relationship makes it work.

Posted August 6, 2026

Freud's famous couch
Source: JRennocks/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0

This is Part 7 of a series that examines the nature of what I refer to as clinical wisdom and provides concrete examples of some of these esoteric secrets of psychotherapy.

For decades, humanistic, existential, Jungian, and other therapists have been touting the importance of the so-called "therapeutic alliance" in predicting successful psychotherapeutic treatment, and, more recently, several scientific studies have corroborated these claims. (See, for example, Wampold et al., 2018 and Opland & Torrico, 2024.) So, the clinical wisdom indicates that this relationship between the patient or client and clinician is crucial and must be treated as such by both. This means that it must be carefully and consciously attended to, nurtured, and cultivated. But what is the true nature of this "therapeutic alliance"? Is it like being with or having a close friend? Lover? Family member? Spouse or significant other? Priest? Rabbi? Cleric? Monk? AI bot? In point of fact, the therapeutic relationship, when appropriately established and properly maintained by the clinician, is unique and unlike any other.

Intimate, Erotic, but Never Sexual

To begin with, the most obvious and best known difference between the relationship between therapist and patient or client and other relationships is the prohibition, both ethically and legally, of any intimate sexual contact during the course of therapy and for at least two years subsequent to termination. There are many good reasons for this, not the least of which has to do with the intense emotional intimacy of the therapy dyad and the intrinsic power differential between patient and therapist, as well as the power of what Freud referred to as transference, which he defined as the unconscious projection of (or transfer onto) the person of the therapist or analyst of the patient's negative or positive feelings about their parents, caretakers, or other significant figures, particularly from childhood. Given the dramatic and global shift in recent years from in-person to remote video therapy, the risks of acting out these sometimes erotic feelings physically are considerably lessened, though not completely eliminated; such sexual, erotic, or romantic feelings can still be pursued and engaged in online or via "sexting" by phone if not in person.

The Corrective Emotional Experience

One of the more obscure secrets about psychotherapy is that love or eros—a specific form of love, life force, desire, relatedness, and close friendship—is always present to some extent, be it consciously or unconsciously, in the therapeutic relationship. Indeed, psychoanalysis, or what some call the "talking cure," the prototypical form of psychotherapy, has curiously also been referred to at times as the "love cure." The love cure. In fact, Freud himself once said, in a letter to Jung, that "psychoanalysis is in essence a cure through love." What did he mean by this? Psychotherapy is essentially an intimate relationship between two people. But it is a totally different kind of connection, unlike lovers, spouses, family, co-workers, or best friends, though not one devoid of caring, compassion, closeness, and, yes, even eros or love.

Another secret is that some (though not all) psychotherapists are formally trained to make deliberate but limited and proscribed use of love's transformative power to help patients heal themselves. How so? Love, like the legendary arrows of Eros or Cupid, can both hurt and heal. Almost always, psychotherapy patients, like most of us, more or less, suffer from having been insufficiently or inappropriately loved (and sometimes this, paradoxically, can include being loved too much) during childhood, adolescence, or adulthood. They commonly suffer from what could be called an excruciating "love wound," which, along with the fear of being hurt, rejected, or abandoned again, manifests neurotically in every aspect of adult life, but especially in their relationships. And it is only love—the right love, at the right time, from the right person, in the right measure—that can heal this agonizing and infuriating injury. Indeed, psychotherapy can be seen as a process in which the patient not only receives love, empathy, acceptance, and compassion from the clinician but, as a consequence, learns to accept and reciprocate such caring and, incrementally, to love and care for themselves and others.

This is similar, if not identical, to what psychoanalysts Franz Alexander and Thomas French (1946) called "a corrective emotional experience," insofar as the patient becomes receptive to the clinician's therapeutic love by dint of permitting themselves to be vulnerable in the psychotherapy process, and finally gets what they needed and wanted but were tragically denied during childhood: understanding, acceptance, compassion, caring, recognition, encouragement, and support, which is as good a definition of real or mature love or eros as I know. Receiving and experiencing love like this from the therapist (or others) can be a healing, liberating, and transformative experience for some. But, while this therapeutic experience of such "unconditional positive regard" from the clinician (see Rogers, 1951 ) is (or should be) part and parcel of every serious course of psychotherapy, it may not be sufficient to magically eliminate the client or patient's distressing signs and symptoms. (See my prior post.)

item.title: Two Dreams, Same Conversation
item.description:
Dreaming

Two Dreams, Same Conversation

How an escalating dream series grabs our attention when we'd rather look away.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • A dream can be an unmistakable reflection of a current daytime struggle.
  • Remembering two or more dreams from the same night is evidence of a continuing conversation.
  • Dream conversations that incorporate escalation can encourage us to take action when we are avoidant.
  • Plays on words and puns are powerful clues for dream analysis.

Bonnie came to me with two dreams from two consecutive nights. Although the dreams seemed unrelated, our analysis showed why they stayed together in her mind: The second dream continued the internal conversation that the first dream began.

The First Dream

"In the first dream, I'm in bed and hear someone lurking around. I call out, 'Who's there?' A woman comes out of the shadows. Although I don't know the woman, I recognize her as someone familiar.

"I get up and see the woman's purse, which is smoking. I grab the purse and open the patio door to throw it in the yard, but then I realize there are flames outside and the house is catching on fire. I come back inside screaming at the woman: 'You set my house on fire!'

"She's standing there, recording me with her phone. She never says a word the entire dream."

The Discussion

I asked, “Are you feeling someone inside your space lately? Maybe not just inside your space, but creating a potential hazard.”

Bonnie answered, “I'm thinking about my niece. My mom has been discussing her lately. Because of that, I feel like she's inside my space.

"My niece is also a bit of a stranger to me. It's just like in the dream. She 'came out of the shadows' recently. Although we are family, we spend very little time together. Every once in a while, I text or message her, but she mostly doesn’t respond."

I wondered, "Does this feel like how you recognize the woman as 'someone familiar' in the dream?"

“It's definitely about her. My mom shared with me the day before the dream that she's very worried about my niece, who is going through a tough time financially. My mom loves her so much. She sent my niece some relief and has been trying to contact her, but hasn't gotten a response in weeks."

I responded, “Considering how protective you are of your mom, I can understand how this incident could feel like it invades your space.”

Bonnie said, “Yes. This bothers me because on the rare occasion that we do see each other, she never puts her phone down. So, I know she sees our texts.”

Bonnie added, "I'm also sure this is about my niece because of the purse. She's been having trouble with money, and in my dream, the purse is smoking. That's almost funny, but not, the way she burns through money."

Next, Bonnie told me about the dream she had the following night.

The Second Dream

"I'm driving, but I stop the car. I try to back up, but something is preventing me. I get out and see my sister on the ground, under the wheels of the car. She looks dead. (My sister passed away five years ago, and my niece is her daughter.)

"Now I'm frantically trying to call 911. The phone doesn't let me dial, and somehow, I have no voice on the phone. I scream at my sister to wake up, and finally she does. I tell her to stay still; I will go get help.

"I run to the nearest street and start asking people to lend me their phone, but the same thing happens. The phone won't cooperate, and I have no voice. I decide to go back to my sister and carry her to the hospital myself.

"I run back to the car, but when I get there, both she and the car are gone."

The Discussion

I commented, "The fact that you cannot get through with the phone or use your voice to get help reminds me of your inability to contact your niece or speak to her."

Bonnie concurred. "Yes, that fits. I'm wondering why both the car and my sister were gone when I returned. It's like the action stopped."

Hearing Bonnie's choice of language, I jumped in. "I'm struck by how you say, 'the action stopped.'"

Bonnie caught her play on words. "That's what happens. She reaches out for financial help to my mom, and when she gets the help, she disappears. My mom is left, not knowing.

"In the second dream, with both my sister and the car disappeared, I am also left not knowing."

"Good observation!" I exclaimed. "Remember, though, your plan was to carry your sister to help. This would have continued the action."

Bonnie reflected, "Yes. Perhaps, even though she may not respond, if I try to reach out to my niece, I would be continuing the action."

I agreed. "You would be treating the dream, where the action stops, as a 'call to action.'"

Bonnie responded, "Perhaps that's the dream's message right there: My lack of voice inside the last dream. Even now, I can feel my ability to speak rising.

"I'm going to reach out to her. Maybe I'll be successful getting her. At the very least, I might be able to give my mom some peace of mind."

What We Can Learn

By describing her dreams out loud, Bonnie caught various plays on words: how her niece "burns through" money and "stops the action," and even how her own inability to speak in her dream ultimately "drives" her to express herself in waking life.

The second dream augments both the urgency of the situation and the theme of speechlessness from the first dream. This intensification illustrates how an interior conversation that began the day before the first dream appears with increasing force in the dreamer's sleep. The escalating conversation through dreams forces the dreamer to notice her lack of speech and opens the door to changing her response. She is now answering the "call to action" by deciding to reach out to her niece.

Given that every dream is, in fact, an interior conversation, the dreamer can change her dream and, in so doing, change her response in the conversation. The simple act of imagining a different response in a dream can help you start to reconsider your inner conversations around difficult issues and guide you toward changing your response in waking life.

item.title: Is Your Son Defiant, or Is He Missing a Skill?
item.description:
Executive Function

Is Your Son Defiant, or Is He Missing a Skill?

When "he won't listen" is really about lagging executive functioning skills.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • What looks like defiance is usually a lack of skillfulness, not willfulness.
  • Challenging behavior appears when a moment's demands exceed the skills a boy has to meet them.
  • The missing skills are executive functions: inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility.
  • Help him by identifying his lagging skills, meet him where he's at, and teach him the skills over time.

Life with a challenging boy is, well, challenging.

You tell your son to get dressed for school, and 10 minutes later, you find him still in his pajamas, watching YouTube. You ask if he’s finished with homework, and he swears he is (even when he's sure to be caught in the lie). You look for his jacket and discover that he’s lost it. The second one he’s lost this year! The smallest frustrations (he doesn't want what's for dinner, he plays badly in a video game) lead to epic meltdowns.

From the outside, it feels irresponsible, oppositional, and disrespectful. Looked at from the inside, however, a different picture emerges.

Over 30 years of working with challenging boys and their families, I have yet to meet a boy who didn't want to do well in school, get along with his siblings and peers, and, more than anything, feel that his parents love him and are proud of him.

So what is going on here?

The Hidden Complexity of “Simple Demands”

Think of everything that your son must do to follow even a small direction like "Time to start your homework":

  • Stop what he's currently doing
  • Process and understand what’s being asked of him
  • Manage his emotions, body, and impulses
  • Shift his attention to his homework

We experience that as one simple ask, but it is actually a multi-step demand.

Psychologist Ross Greene points out that what feels like willfulness is actually a lack of skillfulness. Challenging behavior occurs when the demands of the moment exceed the skills a boy has to meet them.

Most of the time, it's set off by a request that seems ordinary: a parent or teacher asking him to follow a rule or do as he's told. But it can be triggered just as easily by a disappointment (losing a game) or frustration (schoolwork that feels too difficult). When he meets one of those moments without the skills to handle it, he gets emotionally overwhelmed and shifts into fight-or-flight.

Once he's flooded like this, the behavior we find so maddening occurs:

  • He fights: yelling, arguing, or lashing out to make the demand stop
  • He flees: stalling, avoiding, refusing, lying, disappearing into his room

It isn't calculated manipulation, intentional defiance, or him trying to “win.” It's a signal that, in this moment, your son lacks the skills the situation requires.

Executive Functioning: The Lagging Skills

Psychologists call the capacity to manage yourself instead of running on autopilot executive functioning. Our executive functions are the effortful, self-directed thought processes we all use to manage ourselves: our emotions, our attention, our impulses. Without executive functions, we're trapped in automatic, habitual reactions. We can't learn from the past or look to the future, adapt when circumstances change, motivate ourselves, or hold our attention where we want it.

Executive functioning is what lets us shape our lives through intentional choice, rather than being constantly buffeted by forces outside ourselves. It is also exactly what a challenging boy tends to be short on.

Psychologist Adele Diamond argues that there are three core executive functions: inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility.

Inhibitory Control

Inhibitory control is what allows you to stop yourself, and it's the foundational skill that every other form of self-control is built on. Stopping an automatic reaction is what creates the space that enables us to think before we act.

When a boy isn't paying attention, is interrupting, isn't listening, blurts out something hurtful, comes out swinging in a conflict, or keeps putting off what he doesn't want to do, we usually aren't looking at a boy who won't behave. We're looking at challenges with inhibitory control.

Working Memory

Working memory is the ability to hold information in mind so we can work with it. It's what lets us call up a past experience and apply the lesson, and it's what lets us picture a future, set a goal, and make a plan to get there. We use it constantly without noticing: to hold the rules of a game in mind while we play and track our strategy for winning; to connect one paragraph of a reading passage to the next and keep the whole thing in mind long enough to answer a question about it; to carry out a string of instructions like "get dressed, brush your teeth, and pack your backpack for school." It's even the foundation of taking turns; you have to hold in mind that it was my turn a moment ago, so now it's yours.

When a boy loses his water bottle, his headphones, and his homework; when he can't do a chore without nagging and reminders; when he forgets what he was assigned, or forgets to turn it in, or turns it in late; when he isn't ready on time even for something he wants to do; when he doesn't anticipate the consequences of his actions; when he doesn’t get an assignment into his notebook. None of that is opposition or defiance. It's challenges with working memory.

Cognitive Flexibility

Cognitive flexibility is the third core executive functioning skill. To be flexible in his thinking, a boy has to inhibit his current thought, feeling, impulse, or point of view and then hold a new one in mind. It's what lets us change course when a plan isn't working, and to think creatively. It’s also the foundation of empathy, setting our own perspective aside long enough to hold someone else's in mind.

So when a boy won't share or wait his turn, when he melts down because plans changed, when he hits a hard math problem and quits instead of trying another strategy or asking for help—this isn't stubbornness, selfishness, or inconsiderateness. It's a boy whose cognitive flexibility can't yet keep up with what the moment is asking of him.

Shifting Your Perspective to Meet Your Son Where He’s At

Once you start seeing challenging behavior through this lens, a lot of the frustration recedes. The boy who "won't listen," "won't try," and "won't behave" is, far more often than not, a boy whose inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility simply haven't caught up to the demands he’s facing. That isn't an excuse, and it doesn't mean you're stuck, but you do need a plan.

The first step is to stop asking "Why won't he?" and start asking "What's this moment demanding of him that he can't yet do?" The second step is to modify the situation to meet him where he actually is developmentally, rather than where his age says he should be, so the demand stops exceeding his skills. And the third step is to help him develop the lagging skill. Parenting a challenging boy is never about breaking his will. It's about seeing what skills he needs help building.

(Adapted from my book, Challenging Boys: A Proven Plan for Keeping Your Cool and Helping Your Son Thrive.)

item.title: What Is Your Odyssey?
item.description:
Identity

What Is Your Odyssey?

You can apply the psychological lessons of "The Odyssey" to your own life.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • We are all navigating difficult journeys.
  • While there are many pitfalls in life, the journey itself can be rewarding.
  • Challenges make us who we are, especially if we never give up on ourselves.
Source: nonbirinonko / Pixabay

This is less of a movie review and more of a lens through which to view your own personal odyssey. Because you are on an odyssey of your own; we all are. Maybe you are navigating being a parent for the first time. Or perhaps you are on a journey of chronic illness, aging, or grief. Remember: Every story has a beginning, a middle, and an end. No matter where you are in the journey, you have a responsibility to yourself and those around you to be true to what matters in your eyes. For if you are not, you may end up painfully close to where you began in the first place, without much to show for it. As Homer’s Odyssey is both a literal homecoming and a symbolic journey of the soul, here are some takeaways that might help you along the path.

  • The journey itself changes you. Just like Odysseus's, your path will contain triumphs, setbacks, and loss. For many, it will also include trauma, betrayal, and pain. Our course in life changes us. Whether it is for the better or worse is largely up to you. Some become embittered by life’s challenges. Others find a way to accept the changes, even embrace them, without losing sight of the joys that can nearly always be found if you look for them hard enough.
  • Every life has its own Scylla and Charybdis. If you recall, this was Odysseus’ impossible choice. In one direction was the whirlpool that could mean capsize for his vessel. In the other, a six-headed monster that could eat him up. Your dilemma may be less dramatic, but it is equally fraught. Perhaps it is a choice to marry or remain single (both have their challenges), or between two careers—or the mirage of work/life balance. Rarely is one path a clear winner in life.
  • There are lotus flowers everywhere. In the movie, Calypso helped Odysseus forget his trauma by offering him lotus flowers. Of course, this also deprived him of his memories of home and his true identity. Yes, it buried the pain temporarily, but the cost was great—seven years of his life. Your cost might be even greater. What is your lotus flower? Many people dull their pain with drugs or alcohol. Others escape through affairs, work, or food. The largest time suck these days is our phones. Ask yourself, how much time are you losing by turning to social media every day? Better to see yourself and your life for what it truly is. This way, you can remain present while also being true to yourself.
  • You have a bow that only you can string. Each of us is unique. There is something about you that sets you apart from the rest of the world: a talent, an outlook, or a character trait. I urge you to foster this attribute and share it as a gift to yourself and others.
  • There may be something you cannot unsee or undo. Odysseus struggled to move past the horrors of war that he witnessed (and was a party to) in the fall of Troy. Similarly, we have all made mistakes. We may have hurt others or been hurt ourselves. In other words, we all have literal or emotional scars. However, if we learn from our mistakes and alter our path when necessary, we may become less haunted by the past. Of course, true trauma can be assisted by professional support, so there is no need to navigate it alone.
  • Never give up. You will face hardships in life. You will fail. We all do. It is a part of the human condition. However, those who keep moving forward, like Odysseus, ultimately reach their destination. It may not be easy, but it is worth the journey.

item.title: Trust Is Built Long Before It's Ever Tested
item.description:
Trust

Trust Is Built Long Before It's Ever Tested

Trust grows through everyday reliability, not just avoiding betrayal.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • Small moments of follow through shape emotional safety over time.
  • Consistency helps partners feel secure and reduce mental load and resentment.
  • Trust grows through accountability, repair, and keeping everyday promises.

If I were to ask a couple in my office (or even a friend) what trust means, I would probably get some version of the same answer: No cheating, no lying, no secrets, and keeping whatever agreements they've made. And they're not wrong. If a couple agrees to be monogamous and one partner has a physical affair, trust has been broken. There's no gray area there.

Why the Traditional View of Trust May Be Incomplete

But the more I've worked with couples, the more I've found myself pushing back on this definition. I think we've become so focused on how trust gets broken that we've stopped paying attention to how it's actually built. The irony is that by the time trust is tested by something like an affair or a major lie, it's often been quietly built, or eroded, for years. I sometimes wonder if we've misunderstood trust altogether. We talk about it like it's an emotion, but I think it's actually a prediction. Every interaction teaches us a little more about what we can expect from the people we love, and, over time, our brains become really good at forecasting whether someone will follow through. This is why trust feels so intuitive. We are rarely thinking about all the evidence we've collected, but we are responding to the prediction our brain has already made.

As a result, many couples end up sitting in my office confused. Nobody cheated, nobody lied, yet something feels off between them, and no one can quite explain why. I use a simple example in session that has nothing to do with affairs or dishonesty. It has to do with a gallon of milk. Imagine your partner calls while you're driving home and asks if you'll stop at the store. You say sure, and when you walk through the front door, you're carrying it. It's an ordinary moment that neither of you will probably remember a week later because, after all, it's just milk. Now imagine you genuinely forget. When your partner asks about it, you apologize. Most healthy relationships can get through that without much difficulty. Life can be hectic, and we all forget things sometimes. And nobody is asking for perfection.

But what happens when it's not just the milk? Maybe you say you'll make the phone call, but you don't. You say you'll schedule the appointment, and two weeks later it still hasn't happened. You promise you'll take care of something, and eventually your partner does it because waiting has become more frustrating than doing it themselves. Before long, the conversation isn't really about milk anymore. What your partner is learning in those moments as they build up is that they can’t actually count on you.

Redefining Trust as Consistent Reliability

This is really where trust lives. To me, trust isn't simply the absence of betrayal. It's the confidence that the person you love will generally do what they say they're going to do. Their words and their actions line up more often than they don't. That doesn't mean they're flawless; it means they're dependable.

One of the reasons this matters so much is that our brains are constantly looking for patterns. We want to know what we can expect from the people closest to us. When someone is consistently reliable, your nervous system finally gets a chance to relax. You don’t have to send a third reminder text or make a backup plan just in case. And you're not mentally carrying a list of everything that still needs to get done because you're worried it won't happen otherwise. There's a quiet sense of relief that comes from knowing that they said they'd do it, so I don't have to carry it anymore.

When that reliability isn't there, something shifts. I hear one version of this over and over again: One partner starts to feel like the manager of the relationship. They're the one reminding, following up, checking in, planning ahead, and carrying the mental load. The other partner is often genuinely confused because, in their mind, they haven't done anything terrible. They haven't cheated or lied. They just forget stuff sometimes. The problem is that trust rarely disappears because of one missed promise. More often, it slowly erodes through accumulated disappointments until one day someone realizes they don't feel safe depending on their partner anymore. I can't tell you how many times I've heard someone say, "This might sound ridiculous, but I just don't feel like I can rely on them." My response is always the same: That doesn't sound ridiculous at all.

Feeling like you can rely on your partner is one of the foundations of emotional safety. When I know I can count on you, I don't have to spend energy managing you. That frees me up to actually enjoy being with you. It leaves more room for closeness, laughter, spontaneity, and intimacy. While emotional safety doesn't guarantee a great sex life, it's difficult to feel playful, connected, or sexually interested when you're constantly wondering what you'll have to remember, fix, or finish for someone else. And if those disappointments go unspoken for long enough, resentment often starts replacing connection. That's one of the reasons trust can feel so difficult to explain. Most people don't wake up one morning suddenly trusting or distrusting their partner. Those feelings develop gradually, often before we're even consciously aware of them.

None of this is about expecting perfection. Healthy relationships aren't built by people who never make mistakes. In fact, trust is often strengthened by what happens after a mistake. Owning it, hearing and validating your partner’s feelings and experiences, offering a genuine apology instead of becoming defensive, and following through differently the next time. Those moments often build more trust than pretending the mistake never mattered in the first place or becoming defensive. So maybe it's time we broaden the way we think about trust. Keeping the big promises will always matter, but that's only part of the picture. The other part gets built in the moments that rarely receive much attention, like showing up when you said you would, remembering what matters to your partner, following through on the little commitments, and demonstrating over and over again that your word means something.

We often measure trust by asking whether we've avoided the worst things we could do to our partner. I wonder if a better question is whether we've consistently done the ordinary things that allow them to feel safe with us. If your partner had to describe you to a friend, would "reliable" be one of the first words they used? I have a feeling that answer tells us far more about the health of a relationship than whether trust has ever been dramatically tested.
